newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - British Airways has record profits.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - British Airways has record profits.

text.p: British Airways Plc celebrated 10 years in the private sector a day early on Monday with the announcement of record third-quarter pretax profits, marred only by a sharp rise in jet fuel prices which hit operating profits.
It said higher passenger and cargo traffic helped boost pre-tax profits for the three months by 8.7 percent to 113 million pounds ($184.4 million) on sales up 6.3 percent at 2.02 billion pounds.
The pre-tax result for the nine months to December 31 rose to an all-time high of 583 million pounds, up from last year's record 534 million for the same period.
But third-quarter operating profits slipped to 131 million pounds from 152 million a year ago due to higher fuel prices.
BA said operating profits would have been up 23 percent but for a 33.7 percent rise in the quarterly fuel bill to 222 million pounds.
Its share price rose by 13 pence to 599-1/2 pence after the results, which came in ahead of most market forecasts of around 100 million pounds pre-tax for the third quarter.
"The cost items were much better than expected," said analyst James Halstead at brokers Credit Lyonnais Laing.

"These are very, very good results," said Chris Avery at Paribas Capital Markets. However, he cautioned that there were likely to be some costs to come in the full-year results from recently announced job cuts.
BA plans to make a progress report on its campaign to find a billion pounds of annual cost savings when it reports full-year results in May, chief executive Robert Ayling said.

Chairman Sir Colin Marshall said in his results statement that the cost-cutting programme was on track and he expected the trends behind the economic growth and record profits seen in the airline industry in 1996 to continue in 1997.
BA launched a Business Efficiency programme to rationalise operations in September last year.

Since then it has announced various moves to sell off or reorganise parts of the business such as ground services and cargo handling but Ayling said it was too early to give a running tally of savings made so far.

"I think when we report our year-end figures we will be announcing the accumulative effect...and telling people what we are doing and what sort of impact that's going to have year-on-year," he told Reuters in an interview.
But Ayling said much still had to be done if the airline was to remain competitive, saying that operating margins at rival U.S. carriers were higher.
"I am encouraged by the progress that we are making on the Business Efficiency programme but we have a long way to go yet. We are certainly not there yet by any means." he said.
BA's scheduled passenger traffic in the third quarter was up 9.1 percent with the average number of seats sold rising to a record 71.2 percent of capacity from 70.7 percent a year ago.

The airline said the average fare yield for every kilometre flown dipped 1.8 percent due to the strength of sterling but overall the effects of moves in exchange rates on costs and sales were largely neutral.
Fuel prices were the main factor behind a 0.3 percent increase in unit costs which otherwise would have fallen three percent due to increased efficiencies, the airline said.

Marshall did not comment on the proposed alliance with American Airlines except to say BA would also concentrate this year "on completing the regulatory clearance of the alliance with American Airlines and launch the resultant enhanced services across the North Atlantic."

The controversial deal, which would see BA and American controlling more than 60 percent of the British transatlantic market, has come under heavy fire from rival airlines as well as from the European Commission and some consumer groups.
Ayling said the airline now awaited the British government's ruling on the alliance, following a review of the competition issues by Trade and Industry Secretary Ian Lang.
He also hoped Britain and the European Commission could resolve their dispute over who had jurisdiction on the deal.
"The important point to understand is that the British Government is exercising a jurisdiction under the European Community treaties," he told Reuters. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
